# EduSphere — decisions, phase 1 plan, compliance, costs

Approved by Mikey on 2026-09-04 unless marked "proposed".

## Decisions
- Schools remain the core plan. (Considered a pure direct-to-families/home-supplement pivot on 2026-09-05 — weaker core promise since a home tool adds practice time rather than reclaiming school-day time, plus a crowded market with free incumbents like Khan Academy — and decided against pivoting away from schools.)
- Two consent paths, both in scope, sharing the same product: institutional (schools and formally-organized microschools, consenting under COPPA's school exception) and direct-family (homeschool families, via standard parental consent — a parent creates the account, verified the usual way with a payment card). No new build for either; only the signup/consent flow differs.
- Marketing focus is deliberately narrow for now: microschools and homeschool families, because the mastery/reclaim-the-day philosophy is the actual differentiator for them. Marketing to traditional-school families who want supplemental practice on top of normal school is deferred, not rejected — that segment buys on content breadth and price against free incumbents, not philosophy, and the library isn't broad enough yet to win that fight. Self-serve signup isn't blocked to that audience if they find it on their own; the decision is not to spend marketing effort chasing them yet. Revisit once the coverage map is wider and the aligned segments have produced case studies.
- Branching into specialized trades and corporate training stays a goal either way. Already supported structurally: `subject` and `audience` on each course in `logic.mjs` are plain strings, not a K-12-specific enum, exactly so a course can later be "Electrical safety" for "New hires" as easily as "Math" for "Grade 3." No rework needed to add a vertical — just new courses.
- Texas first, so standards alignment is TEKS first; Common Core codes are kept as secondary tags.
- Rostering and sign-in through what schools run (Clever, ClassLink, Google Workspace for Education) are phase 1 requirements, not extras.
- Student identifier = school-issued ID created by an admin or imported from rostering. Students pick from a class list and never type an ID. Admins can edit, rename, deactivate, and merge (a merge is one event that re-tags two histories; nothing is deleted).
- Content: white-glove first (we build early customers' modules), then tiers — Standard (our library + course switches), Plus (AI-assisted upload with admin approval), Enterprise (white-glove onboarding, custom content, SSO, scheduled reports).
- Uploads never design a sequence from scratch: customers place material into a standards-aligned skeleton per grade that is already ordered foundational → advanced; the pedagogy check flags out-of-order material.
- No public ledger (Hedera or other) in the core product. Nothing about a child ever goes on an immutable public chain. Revisit only for anchoring completed credentials, if a customer asks; signed verifiable credentials come first.
- Coverage is proven, not assumed: a coverage map per grade (every standard → modules) with a test that fails while any standard has no module, and a pilot measured against an outside assessment.
- "Wonder" reflection block: open questions with no right answer; typed for readers, pick-a-picture or tell-an-adult for younger children; never graded, never gating; followed by four respectful voices (scientist, artist, grandparent of faith, skeptic) with none declared right, ending on an open question; every prompt and perspective human-approved before publication; must never imply religion or non-belief is wrong.
- Minutes per day is a first-class metric (the efficiency claim). Fun through variety, pictures, and stories — no streak pressure on young children, no dark patterns.
- Design: dark theme as a toggle (default on for educators, light by default for young learners), a modern readable sans (Lexend or Atkinson Hyperlegible), playfulness through color and illustration, no licensed characters. Done after foundations.
- The confidence score is a printed rubric tuned from data, not a copy of any other product's formula.

## Phase 1 plan (needs Mikey's approval before any service is purchased)
- Stack: Python + FastAPI, PostgreSQL, React. Managed Postgres with row-level security so an educator can only read their own students' rows — enforced by the database, not app code.
- Data: `schools`, `classes`, `learners` (ID only), `enrollments`, `courses/modules/questions`, one append-only `events` table (app role: INSERT and SELECT only). Reports are SQL views over `events`; each view's definition is printed on the report; scheduled reports run the same view on a timer and deliver CSV/email.
- Sign-in: class code + pick your ID (+ PIN for older grades); district SSO. No child emails or passwords held by us.
- Backups: the managed database's automated daily backups and point-in-time recovery. No spreadsheets.
- The educator sign-in screen needs a "Forgot password" link once real accounts exist. In the prototype there is only a shared PIN, so there is nothing to recover yet.
- Sign-in fail-safes (raised 2026-09-05, both impossible in the single-device prototype and both real once the app is centralized):
  - Two students signing in as the same person at once: the later sign-in takes over and the earlier session is ended. Both sessions are written to the event log, so an educator can see it happened and when. Whether that also raises an alert is a decision for the pilot, once we know how often it actually occurs.
  - A student picking the wrong name from the list: three protections, in order of cost. The name is shown prominently on the very next screen, so a mistake is visible within seconds. Backing out to the list costs nothing and records no progress against the wrong student. On shared devices, each student gets a short PIN or a picture password, which is how schools already handle this. If work does land on the wrong record, merging is already built and nothing is lost.
- Review scheduling: spaced review across days/weeks using the confidence score (the "reroute by confidence" behavior).
- Voice: device voice now; a paid text-to-speech service is a phase 1 choice (only question text is sent).
- Phase 2 content pipeline (a graph, not a line): Intake → Structurer (modules, order, standards) → checkers: facts (every claim cited), age-appropriateness, coverage (5+ question types, by code) → pedagogy/order check → human lead-admin approval → publish. Any checker can send the draft back with notes. Every step logged. No agent states a fact it cannot cite; practice is computable or sourced. Teacher-suggested edits enter the same flow.

## Compliance rules (every decision is made with these in mind)
- COPPA: schools consent under the school exception; we collect the minimum; parents and schools can request export and deletion; retention is limited to the agreed period.
- FERPA: we act as a school official under a data-processing agreement; data is used only for the school's purposes; never re-shared.
- State laws: Texas student-privacy law and each customer state's equivalent; sign the district's standard data privacy agreement.
- Collected: school-issued ID, class, and events. Never: names, emails, photos, audio, free text from children, ads, trackers. Read-aloud is output only; there is no microphone.
- Before real students: privacy policy, DPA template, parental/school consent flow, review by an education-privacy attorney. Later: a COPPA Safe Harbor program.
- Accessibility: public schools are held to it — readable type, contrast, screen-reader support, captions for any audio.

## When money starts (rough, changeable)
- Phase 0: $0.
- Phase 1 pilot: managed database + small backend host $15–50/month; domain ~$15/year; text-to-speech pennies per thousand characters; content-pipeline AI calls cents to a few dollars per uploaded document.
- Non-software: privacy attorney review (hundreds to a couple thousand dollars); school-required liability insurance; much later a formal security audit (tens of thousands) when a customer requires it.

## Working method (from the Claude Code best-practices guide, adopted)
- CLAUDE.md stays short: commands, rules, gotchas. Detailed how-tos live in `.claude/skills/` and are loaded on demand.
- Every change ends with `./check.sh`; a Stop hook in `.claude/settings.json` runs it automatically (verify the hook with `/hooks` on first use).
- Explore → plan → implement → check for anything larger than a one-sentence diff.
- Larger changes get a fresh-context review by `.claude/agents/reviewer.md`, gaps only.
- `/clear` between unrelated tasks; after two failed corrections, start a clean session with a better prompt.

## Built on 2026-09-04 (free improvements)
- Browser click-through test found and fixed a real bug: the educator's learner list did not refresh during a session.
- Reading course (Kindergarten, Letters): letter names, order, first letters, counting letters, big/small matching — all computable, read aloud, tap only.
- Wonder block: one typed question after fractions mastery, one pick question for kindergarten courses, four voices, closing question; words never stored; counted as reflections on the educator report.

- Transcript: a printable record of every course a student has worked on, kept whether or not the course is still switched on. Courses never opened are left out, because an untouched course says nothing about a student. It carries the school-issued identifier, the modules, the dates and the confidence figures, and nothing a student wrote. That keeps it inside what a school may share under FERPA and what we may hold under COPPA.
- Mastery is defined per module rather than platform-wide. Five questions suits counting to ten; a twelfth grade physics module may want three longer ones. Courses and modules can override both the number asked and the number needed.

- Life skills are suggestions for educators rather than content for students. Nothing is graded, tracked, or shown to a child, which keeps the section outside the student record entirely.
- They are listed as one sequence from earliest to most mature rather than assigned to grades. Grade assignment implies a precision nobody has, and a mixed age classroom has no single grade to look under. The sequence is an order, not a schedule. This also removes most of the reason an administrator would need to edit the list, so editing is not built for now.
- The screen shades each skill from the palest green at the top to deep forest green at the bottom, so the sequence is visible before a word is read. Four stage markers (Early, Growing up, Teen, Nearly grown) break up a long column without splitting the sequence.
- Educators can mark a skill as covered. This belongs to the classroom, never to a student, so no soft judgment about any child enters a record a parent could request. Covered skills are ticked and muted in place rather than moved, with a Hide toggle for when the list gets long. The word is "covered" rather than "complete", because most of these are never really finished.

- Reflection questions require approval by the school before any student sees one. This is the most sensitive content in the platform, so approval is opt in rather than opt out: an unreviewed question simply never appears. An educator reads the prompt, all four voices and the closing question, then approves, removes, or leaves it. Approval can be withdrawn at any time. This is also a selling point worth stating plainly to schools, since no reflection content reaches a child that somebody there has not read.
- There is nothing for an educator to review in a student's own reflection answers, because those are never saved.

- Onboarding asks for a rough starting level (Early years, Elementary, Middle school, High school and beyond) so the placement check begins near the child and an older student never sees pre-K questions. It is a starting point the check adjusts, not a label.
- Only the early years are asked for a sign-in picture, at the moment of adding, and it can be added or changed later from the roster. Pictures are drawn in the app from a fixed set of eight; photo upload is deliberately not offered.
- Courses containing a module that needs a touch screen carry a warning where the educator assigns them.
- For pre-reader courses, finished modules fold behind one star row so the next thing to do is seen first.

- Sign-in pictures are twelve drawn animals on six background colours, seventy-two in all, so a large school never needs two children to share one. Adding a young student suggests an unused picture automatically, and a duplicate is flagged rather than forbidden.
- Operations are written down in docs/RUNBOOK.md: managed services for everything in phase 1, a developer on retainer, a status page, and a downtime procedure that starts with rollback.

- Development in phase 1 is done through Claude Code against this repository, with `./check.sh` as the gate, rather than a developer on retainer. One human (Mikey) holds the production credentials and the three buttons: roll back, restore a backup, post to the status page. A freelancer's name is kept on file for hands-on help by the half day.
- Phase 1 hosting: Supabase for the database and sign-in (managed Postgres, automatic backups, point-in-time restore, a readable dashboard, a signable data processing agreement) and Vercel for the app (deploy from the repository, one-click rollback). Chosen for status pages and rollback buttons a non-technical owner can use.

- Local-first, decided 2026-09-10 in answer to Mikey's question. The record of what happened is the whole truth, so a file holding every record is a complete backup, and restoring it recreates the classroom on any device. This removes the database, the accounts, the hosting bill and, most importantly, any child's record on a server we would have to protect. The cost is a habit: someone presses Download backup, and the app nags after seven days. Restoring merges by student id and joins event logs, so it can only ever add history. A server is deferred until a customer genuinely needs cross-device sync, which is a large-school problem, not a microschool one. Automatic emailing of reports is not possible without a server; a downloaded file the educator emails to themselves is the equivalent.

- Backup cannot email itself without a server. On a phone or iPad the Share button opens the device's own sheet, where Mail is one tap away; elsewhere it downloads. File names carry the device name, the student count and the date (edusphere-ipad-3-12-students-2026-09-10.json) so a folder from ten devices reads at a glance. A touchless auto-save to a chosen file is possible in Chrome and on Chromebooks and is a next step; iPads do not support it.
- Educators stay signed in while active. After twenty quiet seconds a warning appears; after thirty the PIN is asked again (2026-09-11, Mikey's call: five minutes was long enough for a student to reach the settings on a shared device). Any tap or key resets the clock. Returning within five minutes of the last activity skips the PIN.

- Loop-back routing, built 2026-09-10: two failed rounds in a row on a module reopen its nearest prerequisite for a quick check, even one mastered before. The result screen says so in plain words and offers it as the one thing to do. It is recorded as an event so the educator's module story mentions it. The prerequisite graph is what makes this reach across grades once content exists there.
- An educator creates an account once, from a Create account link under Educator Login: they choose a PIN (four to six digits, a convenience lock stored scrambled on the device), name the device, and pick their state, with an i tip explaining why the state matters. After that, Educator Login asks for the PIN and nothing else. The prototype PIN 2468 still opens the door on a device with no account, so testers are never locked out.
- The Classroom page no longer shows the coverage line; the state and a Change state link sit under the i tip beside the roster text.

- Content written 2026-09-10 while Mikey was away: kindergarten math gained one more/one less, joining and taking away (story word problems), comparing numbers, and shapes; kindergarten reading gained letter sounds and rhymes. Every new generator is re-derived independently in the tests from the question's own words, across 300 seeds. Kindergarten math now covers 13 of 18 TEKS standards, kindergarten reading 5 of 10.
- Word lists for reading (SOUND_WORDS, RHYME_FAMILIES) use only words a kindergartener says and hears. Adding to them is how reading content grows; the tests check every combination automatically.

- All states, decided 2026-09-10: a module is the unit and a standard is a label, so every standard in the plan carries a framework (TEKS or CCSS) and every course is mapped to both. An educator chooses their state once at first sign-in; the Classroom page shows coverage against that state's framework. Fifty states plus DC are listed. Adding a framework means adding its codes to the standards, not new content.
- Updates reach educators by opening the site, because the app is served from a static address and holds no accounts. A backup fixture per format version is kept in tests/fixtures and must restore forever.
- Onboarding documents for whoever comes next: CLAUDE.md now opens with a reading order; docs/VISION.md holds the why; docs/ALGORITHMS.md explains every number and marks which are judgements.

- The class view ("Who needs help"), built 2026-09-10: every active student ranked by a need score built only from what is in their record (modules stuck on, loop backs, guessing flags, low confidence on mastered work, time since last practice), with the reasons listed in words so the score is never a mystery, three bands (needs help now, keep an eye on, on track), a one-sentence summary at the top, and Open report on every row.
- The spoken Wonder for pre-readers: one spoken question, large tap targets, two short voices shown one at a time and spoken as they appear, offered once after a mastery and only when approved.

- Letter tracing, built 2026-09-10, is the first touch-screen module and the answer to "how do they learn to write without paper". Twelve capital letters are defined as strokes on a 100 by 100 grid; the pad shows them faintly with a green starting dot and an arrow; the finger's path is checked by arithmetic: every stroke must be visited in order within a tolerance that forgives a wobbly hand, and most of the drawing must lie on the letter so a scribble fails. The Letters course now carries the touch-screen warning. Lowercase letters and curves beyond O and C are the next step.

- Reflection answers stay unsaved, decided again 2026-09-10 after the move to local-first. The legal exposure shrank, but two reasons stand: a child who knows a teacher will read it writes to perform rather than to think, and anything stored travels in backup files that get emailed around. If Mikey wants it, the honest form is an educator switch, off by default, with answers excluded from backups unless explicitly included.
- "Arithmetic, not AI" means: built from checked rules and word lists, never composed by a language model at question time. Open writing is the stated exception: prompts from templates, structure checked by rule, quality judged by a person or an AI assistant with a teacher confirming.
- Browser account sync does not share EduSphere data: browsers sync settings, not a site's storage. One device per student, or restore before switching. Subscription tiers by device count are fine; sync is not to be promised.
- Selling and sign-in without a server of ours: a static landing page with Buy and Log in, purchase through a payment service that issues a license key at checkout, the key checked offline by the app. The only thing maintained is the payment dashboard. The page also lists permissions (allow downloads for backups; no microphone; no account) and device advice (Chromebook or desktop Chrome for touchless backup, iPad for finger tracing).
- Pre-K courses are non-linear: parallel activities where only named prerequisites apply. Pre-K standards come from the Texas Prekindergarten Guidelines and the federal Head Start Early Learning Outcomes Framework.

- Reflection answers: confirmed unsaved, 2026-09-10.
- A vendor-held copy of every backup: declined 2026-09-10. It would make EduSphere the custodian of every child's record from every school, which is the server-side data the local-first design avoids, and it needs a data agreement under FERPA and COPPA. Support instead runs on the school's own cloud folder (touchless backup into Drive) and files shared on request. A per-school opt-in under a data agreement is a phase 1 possibility, after the attorney review.

- The product ships as `index.html`, built by `tools/build-site.mjs` with React bundled in and storage on the browser's localStorage, so GitHub Pages or any plain host can serve it and nothing is fetched at run time. The `.jsx` artifact remains for the chat preview only. A test reloads the standalone page in a real browser and checks a student survives the reload.

- Desktop layout: the content column widens to 720px on screens over 1000px, the welcome card sits lower, and on screens over 1240px a pair of quiet arcs in the logo's green fill the edges without ever touching a tap target. The backup link glows in place when a backup is due, rather than carrying a halo.

- A forgotten PIN is reset only with a backup file of this classroom, decided 2026-09-11 after Mikey pointed out that a student on a shared device could otherwise reset the PIN and tamper with records. Every backup carries a recovery code made when the account was created; the reset checks it. A student does not have the educator's backup file. Each reset is recorded in the profile and shown on the Classroom page. The PIN itself is never in a backup or a file name. Two limits stated plainly: a brand-new account with no backup cannot be reset (the Classroom page nudges for a first backup), and a student who knows browser developer tools can read anything stored locally, which is the floor for any offline app and why the PIN is called a convenience lock.
- Sign out on the Classroom page ends the educator session at once, so the next person at a shared device meets the PIN screen.
- Contact us opens a small popup with the address and an email button, rather than showing the address beside the link.

- The recovery code sits first in every backup file with a note saying what it is for, shows on the Backup page to a signed-in educator, and can be typed on the Forgot PIN screen instead of choosing the file. Nobody has to open a backup to find it, but anyone who does sees it at once.

- Reflections come round after every two mastered modules (Mikey asked for every two or three, 2026-09-11), drawn from a pool shared across courses at the same stage and rotated so the least recently answered comes first. Six more questions were written so the rotation has something to rotate through: three for the early years, three for grades 3 to 5. The logo is now the browser-tab icon, built from the same drawing.

- A reflection question is never offered a third time to the same student (WONDER_MAX_REPEATS = 2), decided 2026-09-11. Once every approved question in a stage has been answered twice, the reflection is skipped rather than repeated. Pool size therefore governs how often reflections appear, never whether one repeats. The pool grew to 36 (17 early years, 19 grades 3 to 5) and should keep growing; the teen and grown stages have none yet because no courses exist there.

- Reflection themes, decided 2026-09-11 from Mikey's list: world (curiosity), failure (failure is how learning happens), feelings (naming and handling them), ups-and-downs (hard days are normal and we get through them, without getting tied up in our own narratives). Every question carries one. The cadence counts finished rounds, pass or fail, not masteries, so a struggling child meets reflections more often; after a failed round the failure, feelings and ups-and-downs questions come first. The pool is 56 and a coverage check notes any stage with fewer questions than modules, so the pool keeps pace as the curriculum grows.

- Three.js is not used, decided 2026-09-11 when Mikey offered it. It weighs about 600 KB and needs a graphics context that some locked-down school devices disable, so it would slow the first load and fail quietly on the machines a microschool is likely to have. The 3D look is achieved with gradients in the SVG drawings we already use (shaded solids and counting balls), which weigh nothing and render everywhere. Three.js stays an option for one specific future screen, such as a solid a child can spin, loaded only there.

- Young learners, redefined 2026-09-11 on Mikey's instruction: a student with ANY early-years course (pre-K to grade 2) still unfinished gets the handheld screens, whatever else is assigned. Early courses list first in every subject, the prerequisite graph keeps advanced work locked until the early work it depends on is mastered, and the star row counts only early modules. Once every early course is complete the student graduates to the regular screens.
- A new student starts on the recommended courses for their level (the two lowest grades of their band), not on every course. Course lists on the report run pre-K first, college last.
- Every user-facing string is checked for American spelling and house style by tests/spelling.test.mjs (step 3 of check.sh). Contractions are welcome. Mikey's exact wording is never overridden once given.
- The educator report: a collapsible bulleted summary (open by default), a collapsible Assigned now list (closed), all per-course progress behind one Progress by course dropdown with an i tip (closed), and Key Words - Explained with each term folded until tapped. Reviewed Wonder questions fold under a Reviewed row per stage so the next awaiting question is always at the top. Every i tip shares one gradient look and closes on sign out and on leaving a screen.

- index.html stays one generated file on purpose: it runs from GitHub Pages, a USB stick or a double-click with nothing to fetch, and its length costs nothing because nobody edits it. The sources are already split (src/logic.mjs, src/curriculum.mjs, src/ui.jsx) and those are what get edited.
- New students start on the lowest grade of their band only (pre-K for early years). Finishing every module of a course switches on the next course up in that subject automatically, recorded as a courses_enabled event so the educator sees it and can change it. A placement check, once built, will jump further.
- Young learners' subject cards breathe (a gentle scale and soft shadow on the card itself) instead of carrying a halo that grew beyond the screen; locked modules are not shown to them; the finished-modules fold sits below the available modules. Reflection screens open with a sliding "Let's Wonder!" title. The matching lesson shows two shapes side by side.
- The test browser runs with reduced motion, because a card that breathes forever never looks still to an automated click.

- The zip is the repository: it unpacks without a wrapper folder and contains exactly what GitHub should hold (no dist/). A .gitignore keeps .DS_Store and test output out. The tab icon is a bold drawing of its own (green disc, gold arc, white E) because the full logo's arcs vanish at sixteen pixels. On laptops the welcome page is a full-height column: logo a third bigger, a taller sign-in box, the three links at the foot and larger, and the side arcs wider; the pointer fades letters as well as arcs.

- Wide screens (2026-09-11): the content column zooms by 8 percent so text and taps grow together, sections get more air, the Classroom intro is padded to wrap in two lines with the i kept on the line, Wonder Questions and Life Skills sit side by side, the Active Students dropdown and its list share one box, Add someone new and Who needs help narrow to 380px, and the backup link is larger. Phones are unchanged.
- A pre-K reading course (rhymes, first sounds, big letters; readAloud; non-linear) so early learners start with both subjects, mapped to the Texas Prekindergarten Guidelines and Head Start; with its own reflection.
- GitHub: publish the unzipped folder itself as the repository through GitHub Desktop (Add Local Repository, create a repository here, Publish); updates are drag-over-replace then Commit and Push.

- Young learners see only their early-years courses on the overview (2026-09-11): anything above grade 2, even if assigned, waits until every early course is complete. Their overview is a full-height column with the greeting centered and larger, no course labels between modules, a star row at the foot that fills from the left like counting, and the practice-again fold beneath the stars. Tapping an answer plays a soft two-note blip made by the browser itself; moving on is silent. The voice prefers warm female voices and speaks a little brighter.
- Welcome page: Educator Login is a green button, the sign-in card is calmer, and the name grid scales with the number of students. The logo's pointer fade is tighter so smaller pieces vanish, and the side arcs draw themselves in once.

- A student record with no course decision gets the starter set for the student's level the first time it is opened (withStarterCourses), so students added before the starter rule are not handed every course. The privacy note sits at the very foot of the welcome page; the PIN screen sits lower on large screens; Who needs help matches Add someone new with its explanation under an i; the Key Words card is darker.

- Spoken lesson lines read like a person talking (2026-09-11): every line must contain a real sentence of four or more words unless it only names letters or counts aloud, and every picture must match the words spoken over it (a shown word is said, a shape is named, a highlight appears in every word shown). Instruction lines are exempt from the word match because a reading lesson must show a word without saying it. tests/scripts.test.mjs enforces both and is step 4 of check.sh. Thirty-seven lines were reworded, such as "Cat. Hat. These two words have endings that sound alike."
- Letter pictures can carry a highlight ('at' for a rhyme ending, 'first' for an opening sound); those letters turn gold and grow while the rest stay quiet.
- Better voices, phase 1 plan: record every fixed spoken line once with a high-quality service at build time and ship the audio with the site, keeping the device voice as the fallback and for prompts whose numbers change. Not built now because it needs a paid key and a network.

- Young learners have no practice-again list (2026-09-11, Mikey's call). Mastered modules return by themselves as memory checks inside later rounds, a child that age does not self-direct review, and a teacher who wants a module redone resets it from the report. The star row stays as the only thing at the foot of their overview.

- Halos are gone everywhere (2026-09-11, Mikey's call): an inviting button pulses itself gently (edu-pulse, a five percent scale) instead of casting a ring around it. The Let's Wonder! title bounces in and shimmers between green and gold. The voice is a little slower (rate 0.86). Two faint spheres drawn from the logo's own arcs flank it on large screens. Wonder Questions and Life Skills cards are green and light gold with their buttons aligned at the foot.

- Cross-course prerequisites gate a module only when the earlier course is assigned to the student (2026-09-11, after Mikey found an Elementary student locked out of every grade 3 reading module). Placement is the educator's judgment: leaving grade 2 off means the student is past it, so grade 3 opens. In-course chains always hold, and loop-back still uses the full prerequisite list, so a struggling student is sent back to the earlier module regardless. gatingPrerequisites and moduleStatuses(progress, enabledIds) carry this; the report, class view and student summary use it.

- While an educator is signed in, a small chip at the top right of every educator screen counts down to sign-out ("Logging out in 30 seconds"); mouse movement, wheel, scrolling, typing and clicking reset it. Touchless backup reports what it last did on the Classroom page and the Backup page, and a failed write switches it off with a visible note instead of silently. The Hear it again control is a speaker button in the top-right corner of the card, and the "on silent" note sits at the foot of the page once anything has been spoken.

- After an idle sign-out, unlocking with the PIN returns the educator to the page and scroll position they were on; Change state does the same. A completed course on the transcript names the standards it satisfied in the state's framework (Common Core until a state is chosen), read from the curriculum plan; a coverage check requires every course to map to at least one code in each framework.

- Touchless backup writes into a chosen folder, one file per day named by the date and rewritten through the day (2026-09-12, answering Mikey's question about a file per module). A backup holds the whole classroom, so a file per completed round would run to thousands of files and gigabytes; daily snapshots give history at a few megabytes a year for a large class. Where a browser offers a file picker but no folder picker, the older single rewritten file is used.

- Touchless backup remembers its folder across browser restarts (the folder handle is kept in the browser's own store, 2026-09-12, after Mikey pointed out that a folder forgotten at every restart made the feature a false promise). After a restart the Classroom page checks: where the browser has kept its permission the daily files resume by themselves; otherwise a single Resume touchless backup tap grants it again. The wording everywhere now says exactly that. A truly unattended backup with no tap on any device would need a server, which is deferred.

- Grade 4 reading (summarizing, making inferences, similes and metaphors, how a text is built; six built passages with summaries, inferences and clues) and grade 5 math (adding and subtracting decimals, multiplying fractions, dividing by two-digit numbers, volume, order of operations) added 2026-09-12 in the same shapes as every other course: five generators per module, every math generator re-derived independently, standards mapped to TEKS and Common Core and marked ready, a reflection per course. 74 modules, 76 reflections. ## 2026-09-25 (pass DQ): the security pass

- Still not committed: this commit message covers DK to DQ, and the changes zip carries all seven passes' files.
- Reviewed: no eval or runtime code building; no network calls anywhere in the app; React draws all user text; the weekly-notes print sheet escapes names and notes before building its markup; the service worker handles only same-origin GET requests. Nothing needed changing there.

A counted try does not wipe a half-typed PIN, and the countdown starts fresh with each lock.
- A Content Security Policy meta in the page head (tools/build-site.mjs): own-site scripts, styles, workers and connections only, data and blob images, data fonts, no plugins, no base changes, no forms. Tested on the real page over a local server: account creation, the classroom and the service worker all work with no policy violations. The Claude preview copy drops the line, since that host frames pages with its own rules.
- Not changed, and said plainly in docs/SECURITY.md: the PIN scramble is simple and a PIN is short, so the device is the real boundary; student PINs are stored as typed; backups are unencrypted files. Encrypted backups and a slower salted PIN scramble are listed for later.

## 2026-09-26 (pass EF): desktop dragging, an empty Notes section, centering, quick checks wording

- Mikey committed DV to EE; this commit message starts fresh at EF.
- Dragging on a desktop (Mikey: nothing dragged, though a long press looked as if it would). In Chromium a mouse drag already worked, so the fault was in what other browsers do with a mouse press: it can start the browser's own selection or picture drag, which cancels the pointer before a game sees it move, and Safari can refuse pointer capture, which threw inside each game's start and stopped the drag before it began. Every drag start now goes through grabPointer: it prevents the default, asks for capture inside try/catch (moves over the board still bubble to it), and the board adds WebkitUserSelect and WebkitTouchCallout none; a document listener stops dragstart inside any game board. Nine drag starts use it (seven games, the two mazes and the drawing pad).
- tests/e2e/drag.mjs, a new check.sh step: a desktop mouse drags a piece, selection is off, the browser's own dragstart is prevented inside a board, and a drag still works when setPointerCapture throws. Against the old code the last two failed, which is the proof the fix addresses the fault.
- The report's Notes card takes edu-no-print when the student has no notes, so it stays on screen for writing one and leaves the printed report. My Completed Skills and its hide checkbox are centered. The quick checks paragraph uses Mikey's words with a line break before the second sentence.

- Mikey: the drag he meant was reordering students on My Classroom, not the games. EF is treated as not yet committed, so this commit message covers EF and EG, and the changes zip carries both passes' files.
- The fault: each card listened for its own pointer moves, and only the held card acted on them. A finger is captured by the card it first touched, so phones worked; a mouse is not, so once the pointer left the held card its moves went to other cards and were ignored. Letting go anywhere drops; a second end is ignored. Text selection and the browser's own dragstart are stopped while a card is held, a right click does not start a hold, and holding near the top or bottom 70 pixels of the screen scrolls the page. The drop now always lands where the line shows (before, dragging downward placed the card one row later than its line).
- tests/e2e/drag.mjs gained three checks: a held card follows a desktop mouse, letting go below the others moves the student to the end, and the new order is saved in the roster. ## 2026-09-29 (pass FT): the plain AI course, for the 6 to 8 band

- The course: `tech-6`, What a machine learns, four modules in order: learning-from-examples (a program shown thousands of labeled examples keeps the patterns they share; the result is a model, a generalization, and a language model builds an answer one likely word at a time), wrong-and-sure (a model's number is fit, not truth; a made-up date that looks right is a hallucination; sounding sure is a pattern too; a second source, and the question how do you know?), fair-examples (a model knows only its examples; the unfairness was in the pile before the model ran; look at who is missing and test on every group), staying-in-charge (the text box is a postcard; a digital footprint; the work inside is someone's intellectual property, and copyright says who may copy it; use the tool to learn, not to skip learning). Six questions a module, every answer said in its lesson first; the untaught report reads zero.
- Standards from TEA's breakouts for §126.17 (grade 6, adopted 2022): (1)(B) patterns in representations of data, (1)(C) abstraction and generalized against specific information, (6)(A) inferences from data, (9)(D) information exaggerated or misrepresented online, (9)(A) safe, ethical and positive online behavior, (8)(A) the digital footprint, (9)(B) intellectual property including copyright, (4)(C) transferring knowledge to new technologies; CSTA level 2: 2-DA-09, 2-DA-08, 2-IC-21, 2-IC-23, 2-IC-20. ## 2026-10-01 (pass HI): the Key idea card, and two questions answered

- Mikey has not committed HD to HH, so the commit message covers HD through HI.
- The Key idea card: in the dark theme it now uses the light green of the mastered lists and notes (#AAD8C5) with dark text (#16201B), and its title and text are centered in both themes; the light theme keeps its gold, as the frozen light theme requires. The click-through checks the color, the dark text and the centered title.
- Licensing, explained in `docs/LICENSING-AND-HOSTING.md`: the app checks codes with a public key, which cannot create codes, so shipping it is safe; the private key must never be in any repository, and the development key's private half in `tests/fixtures/` must be replaced by a real pair before launch. A code that runs only in the browser cannot stop sharing, editing the app, or reading the paid lessons, which today ship inside the one page. The stronger options, online activation and serving paid lessons only after activation, both need a small server and an honest change to the privacy note. Recommendation: launch with names and dates on codes, and build the server option when the curriculum is the asset to protect.
- Hosting, explained in the same doc: a private repository hides the source history and docs but not the built page every browser downloads. Cloudflare Pages and Vercel both deploy private repositories; Vercel's free Hobby plan is non-commercial only (Vercel's fair use guidelines), so a product that sells licenses needs Pro, while Cloudflare's free plan allows business use. Devices load the site the same way on either. The real cost is the move: saved data lives per web address, so every device needs a backup at the old address and a restore at the new one, once, to the permanent domain.
- Next: a college course (proposed Business Principles, anchored to BUSI 1301 in Texas's Academic Course Guide Manual, read before citing), then pictures.

## 2026-10-01 (pass HQ): the refresh test's real cause, found and fixed

- Mikey said "continue" without a commit word, so the last passes count as uncommitted and the commit message covers HM through HQ. Pass HP's files and preview were handed over at the start of this turn; the tool limit had cut the previous turn off just after packaging.
- The intermittent failure of "a refresh brings the student back to the lesson they were on" (four times since pass HG) is explained. A probe cut from the click-through, run six times with every stored key and event count printed around the reload, failed twice, and both times the store was empty after the reload: the student's record and the where-note were gone, though both were present a moment before and nothing in the app or the test page deletes them. The test's stand-in for durable storage is localStorage, and Chromium commits a page's localStorage writes in batches; the reload sometimes started before the newest batch was committed, so the new page opened with an empty store and the app correctly fell back to the welcome screen.
- The earlier explanations were wrong, and are corrected here: pass HM blamed a race with the welcome screen (reading the note first is still sound, but was not the cause), and pass HO blamed a record not yet saved (the record had been saved; the store itself came back empty).
- The fix is in the test, because real storage is durable: before the reload, the test copies the whole store and registers a one-time script that puts back any missing key when the page reloads, guarded by a token in window.name, which survives a reload. The probe was deleted.
- Open item: on a real phone, answer a question and refresh at once, to confirm a real browser never drops the newest answer the way headless Chromium can.
- Next: General Psychology at the college level (PSYC 2301), then the other college courses, one per pass.

The cause was general: a round draws ten questions from a module's banks, and the builder retried a duplicate only sixteen times before keeping it, so any module whose banks hold fewer different questions than its round had to repeat. An audit (tools/question-pools.mjs, report in docs/QUESTION-POOLS.md) found 137 of 603 modules in that position, in every subject.
- Now no round repeats a question: when a bank has nothing new, the module's other banks are tried, and if none has a new question the round ends early. Mastery already scales with the questions actually asked (coreTotal), so a shorter round keeps the same bar. The memory checks and placement probes skip a slot instead of repeating. The two agriculture banks from the screenshots grew from 7 questions to 13, every answer taught in its lesson, which leaves 135 short modules.
- Moving forward: the rules test builds rounds for every module and fails on any repeat, and a ratchet test fails if more than 135 modules fall short, so no new course can add a short bank and the limit only moves down as banks grow. Every new module needs at least as many different questions as its round, and a few more so repeat rounds vary.
- Growing the 135 short banks is now a standing program, a batch of modules per pass, each new question's answer taught in its lesson.
- Next: grow the short question banks, a batch per pass (the report lists them), then General Psychology at the college level (PSYC 2301) and the other college courses.

## 2026-10-01 (pass HS): what counts as a repeat, and the first batch of banks grown

- Mikey has not committed HR, so the commit message covers HR and HS.
- Pass HR's no-repeat rule judged two questions the same when their words matched, which was wrong for picture tasks: "Tap the bigger one" with two different pairs of pictures is two questions. Under that rule a pre-K round of five such tasks stopped after two. One definition now decides what a repeat is, `questionKey` in logic.mjs: the setup, the wording, the picture, the answer and the set of answers offered, in any order. Rounds, memory checks, placement probes, the audit and the rules tests all use it, and the pre-K round is back to five.
- Tracing and dot-to-dot tasks (type trace) are motor practice with no answer to give away, so tracing a letter twice is allowed, and modules made only of tracing are left out of the audit.
- Four early modules teach a two-way contrast by design (red and blue, one and two dots, A and B, sun and moon), so four different questions is the honest maximum and their rounds run four instead of five. Growing them would mean new picture variety, such as different red and blue objects, which is a decision for Mikey.
- First batch grown, the seven core grade 6 modules: mean, median and mode and the four quadrants gained computed questions (new numbers and new points each round, hundreds of different questions); plot and conflict, poetry, microscopes and the supply chain gained fixed questions with every answer taught in the lesson; plate tectonics gained a small fixed bank. ## 2026-10-03 (pass IS): Wonder questions for younger learners, failure and hard feelings first

- Mikey committed through IR and opened a new chat (The Wise Human 3.0), so the commit message starts again at IS. The first attempt at this pass ran out of room after its research; this one wrote it.
- A miss from pass IK, owned and fixed: IK's entry says the unsourced claim that feet find a beat before hands was removed from w-early-lost-the-beat. It left the scientist's written voice but stayed in the line pre-readers hear aloud. That line now says Tap your foot first. Then your hands can follow., which matches the written advice and claims nothing.
- Pre-readers now hear the choices. The Wonder screen for children who cannot read spoke the question but never the choices, and a tap answers at once, so a child chose blind (a code comment said the choices were read aloud; they were not). Now the question is read, then each choice in turn with Or before the last, and the choice being read lights up; Say it again repeats all of it (wonderSpokenParts in logic.mjs, wonderLit in ui.jsx). A rules test holds every spoken early question to its choices.
- Twenty-four new questions, listed here for Mikey's approval; like every Wonder question, none reaches a student until an educator approves it in the app. Early questions are shared across the whole early stage, so each had to make sense to a three-year-old and an eight-year-old alike; their choices stay short enough to hold in mind when heard.
- Early, failure: You spilled water on your picture. Is it ruined? / You tried and tried to zip your coat, and it kept getting stuck. What now? / You colored outside the lines. Is that a mistake? / You kicked at the ball and missed it. What do you do next? / Your shoes are on the wrong feet. Is that a big mistake?
- Early, feelings: When you miss someone you love, what can you do? / Your friends are playing a game and did not ask you. How do you feel? / When a feeling gets very big, can slow breaths help it get smaller? / Is it okay to feel shy when you meet someone new? / A grown-up said no to something you really wanted. What helps the cross feeling?
- Early, hard days: A job feels long and boring, and you want to stop. What could help you keep going? / When you are very tired, do little problems feel bigger?
- Growing, failure: You were completely sure of an answer, and it turned out to be wrong. How did that feel, and what did you do next? / Your team lost, and your mistake was part of the reason. What do you say to your team? / You practiced a piece all week, and at the recital your fingers froze. Does that mean the practice was wasted? / Your writing came back covered in corrections. Is that a bad sign? / You tried out for a team or a play and did not make it. What would you do next?
- Growing, feelings: Sometimes a voice in your head says you are bad at something. Do you have to believe it? / Why can one mean comment stick in your mind longer than ten nice ones? / You found out about a party you were not invited to. What do you do with that feeling? / Your heart races before a test or a game. Is that feeling helping you or getting in your way? / When you make a mistake, what do you say to yourself? Would you say the same thing to a friend?
- Growing, hard days: When you are bored, should you grab a screen right away, or let your mind wander for a while? / On days after you slept badly, does everything seem to go wrong?
- The research behind the claims, read before use: the Batman effect (White, Prager, Schaefer, Kross, Duckworth and Carlson, Child Development 2017: 180 children aged four and six kept at a boring task longest when they pretended to be a hard-working character); a skipped nap (Berger and others, Journal of Sleep Research 2012: toddlers showed more upset and fewer smiles, a small study of ten children); less sleep at 8 to 12 (Vriend and others, Journal of Pediatric Psychology 2013: an hour less for four nights weakened emotion regulation, enjoyment, memory and attention); the hypercorrection effect (Butterfield and Metcalfe 2001, replicated with children); self-distancing in fifth graders (Kross and others, Emotion 2011); self-compassion at 10 to 19 (Marsh, Chan and MacBeth, Mindfulness 2018, nineteen studies; a link, not proof of cause, and the skeptic says so); being left out in the Cyberball game (Hartgerink and others, PLOS ONE 2015, 120 studies); the negativity bias and its early start (Vaish, Grossmann and Woodward, Psychological Bulletin 2008); long breaths out (Balban and others, Cell Reports Medicine 2023, adults); the spotlight effect (Gilovich, Medvec and Savitsky 2000); feedback (Hattie and Timperley 2007); the default mode network (Buckner, Andrews-Hanna and Schacter 2008).
- Mikey's authors, attributed and paraphrased: Michael Singer (you are not the voice in your head; you are the one who hears it), Rick Hanson (stay with a good moment for a few extra seconds and let it sink in), Arthur Brooks (boredom turns the mind toward big questions, framed as his argument).
- Told honestly where the evidence is thin: saying I am excited made people feel more excited in Alison Wood Brooks's 2014 study, but a 2025 direct replication found no change in how they performed, and a 2024 review of 44 results found a small average help, mostly in adults (Bosshard and Gomez, Scientific Reports), so the racing-heart question says the help was small and mostly studied in grown-ups. A few studies found more ideas after boredom, and the question says not every study agrees. Inner speech varies a lot between people, and whether anyone has none at all is disputed (Nedergaard and Lupyan 2024 and a 2025 reply), so the question says only that it varies.
- The pool: 299 questions (early 83, growing 76, teen 62, grown 78); failure and feelings now early 45 and growing 39. One per module would take 304 more (early 84, growing 59, teen 66, grown 95).
- Checks: rules 1,887 and spelling 77; check.sh steps 1 to 11 passed in one run (browser click-through 300), and the turn ended before steps 12 and 13, which then passed on their own (dark theme 55, standalone page 8).

## 2026-10-03 (pass IW): Wonder questions for teens and adults, failure and hard feelings first

- Mikey has not committed IS to IV, so the commit message covers IS to IW. His phone review list finished with IV, so the Wonder pool program resumes, with the older stages this time and his authors.
- Twenty new questions, listed here for approval; none reaches a student until an educator approves it in the app.
- Teen, failure: You got a test back covered in red marks. Did you read the mistakes, or shove it in your bag? Why? / You froze when it was your turn to speak, and now the next time scares you even more. How does anyone get braver? / Before a big project, imagine it is already finished and it failed. What went wrong? / You got a bad grade and hid it from your family. Now it feels worse than the grade did. What now?
- Teen, feelings: The writer Michael Singer says you are not the voice in your head, but the one who hears it. What would change if that were true? / The psychologist Rick Hanson says the brain is like Velcro for bad experiences and Teflon for good ones. Is that true of yours? / Something embarrassing happened weeks ago, and your mind keeps replaying it. Why does it do that, and how do you make it stop? / Your best friend is moving far away. How do you say goodbye, and how do you stay friends?
- Teen, hard days: The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote in his private notebook that what stands in the way can become the way. Is something in your way right now? / You woke up in a bad mood for no clear reason. Do you have to stay in it all day?
- Grown, failure: A Princeton professor named Johannes Haushofer published a CV of his failures: the programs, jobs and grants he did not get. What would yours list, and why might sharing it help someone? / Years from now, which will you regret more: a try that failed, or a try you never made? / You have put two years into something that is not working. Is the time you already spent a reason to keep going? / One study found people learned as much from other people's failures as from their successes, but less from their own. Whose failures have taught you the most?
- Grown, feelings: Michael Singer asks readers to imagine the voice in their head as a roommate who talks all day long. Would you keep a roommate like that? / Rick Hanson argues that lingering on good experiences for a few extra seconds helps them stick. Is noticing the good a real skill, or a way of fooling yourself? / When did you last feel awe, and what did it do to the worries you brought with you? / You sent a message and heard nothing back for a day. What story did you tell yourself about why?
- Grown, hard days: Viktor Frankl, a psychiatrist who survived the Nazi camps, wrote that one freedom can never be taken away: the freedom to choose your attitude. Do you believe that? / On a heavy day, does moving your body change your mind?
- The research behind the claims, read before use: learning less from one's own failure (Eskreis-Winkler and Fishbach, Psychological Science 2019; a 2025 commentary argues the task confounds consistency with learning, so both questions say to hold it loosely); regret (Gilovich and Medvec 1994 and 1995, with the 1998 resolution with Kahneman that many long-term regrets are wistful); exercise and depression (Noetel and others, BMJ 2024, 218 trials, with the authors' own caution about trial quality); awe and the small self (Piff and others, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 2015: the eucalyptus grove and the drops of colored water in milk); Johannes Haushofer's CV of failures (2016, crediting Melanie Stefan's 2010 Nature article); the sunk cost effect (Arkes and Blumer 1985); the liking gap (Boothby and others, Psychological Science 2018); rumination (Nolen-Hoeksema); secrets weighing through mind-wandering (Slepian and others 2017); self-distancing and self-talk by name (Kross and others); inner speech varying between people (Nedergaard and Lupyan 2024); exposure in small steps; desirable difficulties.
- Mikey's authors, attributed and exact: Viktor Frankl (the last of the human freedoms, to choose one's attitude, from Man's Search for Meaning, quoted only in those six words and read against the book's passage); Marcus Aurelius (what stands in the way can become the way, a paraphrase of Meditations 5.20, his private notebook); Aristotle (we become brave by doing brave acts, Nicomachean Ethics II); Michael Singer (you are not the voice but the one who hears it; the inner roommate; letting the noise pass, from The Untethered Soul); Rick Hanson (Velcro and Teflon; a few extra seconds with the good, from Hardwiring Happiness). The often quoted Frankl line about a space between stimulus and response is not used: it is not in his books.
- Honest limits, said in the questions themselves: the failure study is a lead, not a law; bold claims about rewiring the brain run ahead of the savoring evidence; Frankl's freedom is not a test that struggling people have failed; exercise sits alongside therapy and medication, not instead of them; a bad mood that keeps returning for weeks is worth telling a trusted adult, and a heavy season deserves a doctor or counselor.
- The pool: 319 questions (early 83, growing 76, teen 72, grown 88). One per module would take 284 more (early 84, growing 59, teen 56, grown 85).

What do you do? / Your paper airplane crashed right away. What do you do next? / You broke your friend's toy by accident. What do you do? / You tried to help wash the dishes, and water went everywhere. Was helping a mistake?
- Early, feelings: You woke up from a scary dream. What helps you feel safe again? / A thunderstorm is booming outside. What helps when you feel scared? / You need a shot at the doctor. What helps you feel brave? / Someone grabbed your toy without asking. What do you do? / A fun trip got canceled because of the rain. What helps the sad feeling?

What now? / You told a small lie to stay out of trouble, and now you have to keep remembering it. Was it worth it? / You want to quit your team or your lessons in the middle of the season. Is quitting the same as failing? / You were sure your project would take one evening, and it took three. Why does everything take longer than we think?
- Growing, feelings: Some people say hitting a pillow gets your anger out. Does it? / After you do something wrong, do you think "I did a bad thing" or "I am a bad kid"? Is there a difference? / Your friend won the prize you wanted. Can you feel happy for them and sad for you at the same time? / Some people say crying is for babies. Is it? / Is waiting for something scary, like the dentist or a big test, sometimes worse than the thing itself?
- Growing, hard days: A test, a fight with a friend and a sick pet, all in one week. What do you do when hard things pile up? / At the end of a hard day, can you still find three good things?
- Owned and fixed, three answers that recommended venting a feeling. My own artist line in pass IS (w-early-grown-up-said-no) said feelings need somewhere to go and suggested stomping out a drum beat or squeezing a pillow, and two older lines framed drawing as getting a feeling out (w-early-feeling-sad: the feeling has somewhere to go; w-angry-feeling: getting it out of your body). The evidence points the other way: in Bushman's 2002 study, angered people who hit a punching bag while thinking about whoever angered them ended up angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing, and a 2024 review of 154 studies (Kjaervik and Bushman, Clinical Psychology Review) found that calming activities reduce anger while arousing ones mostly do not, jogging least of all. With children aged 6 to 12, drawing something new lifted a sad mood more than drawing what had upset them (Drake and Winner, Cognition and Emotion 2013). New text, for approval: w-early-grown-up-said-no: "When I feel cross, I draw something I love, like a garden or my dog, and my busy hands help my mind settle. In one study, children who drew something new felt better than children who drew what had upset them." / w-early-feeling-sad: "Some people draw something they love when they feel sad, like a pet or a favorite place. In one study, that helped children feel better more than drawing the sad thing did." / w-angry-feeling: "Putting a feeling on paper turns it into something you can look at and name, instead of something that pushes you around.". A rules test now reads every Wonder voice for venting advice, and CLAUDE.md carries the rule.
- The research behind the claims, read before use: needles (Birnie and others, Cochrane 2018: 59 trials, 5,550 children; distraction, breathing, hypnosis and combined CBT help, with low-quality evidence, which the question says); helping (Warneken and Tomasello, Science 2006: 18-month-olds help a stranger without being asked or rewarded); intent and accidents (Cushman and others, Cognition 2013: intent-based judgment grows between 4 and 8, accidents judged leniently by about 8); speech sounds (Crowe and McLeod 2020: most English consonants by 5, the th in thumb at about 6); bad dreams (the AAP and AASM: most common from about 3 to 6, up to half of young children wake a parent); thunder (National Weather Service: five seconds per mile, when thunder roars, go indoors); waiting (Mischel and Ebbesen 1970 and Mischel, Ebbesen and Zeiss 1972; Kidd, Palmeri and Aslin 2013: about 12 minutes against 3 with a reliable grown-up; Watts, Duncan and Quan 2018: the link to later life about half the original and two thirds smaller after controls); the checklist (Haynes and others, NEJM 2009: eight hospitals, complications 11 to 7 percent, deaths 1.5 to 0.8 percent, a before and after study); the planning fallacy (Buehler, Griffin and Ross 1994: 33.9 days guessed, 55.5 taken, fewer than half done by the worst-case guess; unpacking a task into steps helps, Kruger and Evans 2004); lying (Talwar and Lee: most children peek and many deny it, and younger ones blurt out the toy's name); quitting (Angela Duckworth's Hard Thing Rule, Grit, pages 241 and 242); guilt and shame (Stuewig, Tangney and others 2015: 380 fifth graders followed into young adulthood); mixed feelings (Larsen, To and Fireman, Psychological Science 2007, ages 5 to 12); crying (Bylsma, Vingerhoets and Rottenberg 2008: 5,096 students in 35 countries; comfort helps a cry help, shame and suppression make it less likely; about a third report no change); dread (Berns and others, Science 2006: most chose a shock sooner, and 9 of 32 took a stronger one sooner rather than wait); a bedtime to-do list (Scullin and others 2018: 57 young adults fell asleep faster); three good things (Seligman and others 2005, with White and others, PLOS ONE 2019: effects smaller than first reported); kintsugi; the Wright brothers' 1901 wind tunnel (about two hundred wing shapes) and Wilbur's 1908 admission to the Aero-Club de France that in 1901 he had told Orville people would not fly for fifty years; Judith Viorst's Alexander and the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Day (1972), paraphrased.
- One of Mikey's thinkers, exact: Socrates, paraphrased from Plato's Apology 21d (wiser in one small way: he did not think he knew what he did not know). The popular line "I know that I know nothing" is not in Plato and is not used.
- Said honestly in the questions themselves: the needle studies were not perfect; waiting well at four does not decide a life; the three good things effect is smaller than first reported, worth a try and not magic; crying does not help about a third of the time; the to-do list finding "seems to" work. For Mikey, not in the text: the checklist study compared before and after rather than randomizing, and the guilt and shame study shows a link, not proof of cause.
- The pool: 343 questions (early 95, growing 88, teen 72, grown 88); failure and feelings now early 55 and growing 49. One per module would take 260 more (early 72, growing 47, teen 56, grown 85).

- The lessons called ( ) brackets, as British English does. American math, the TEKS (5.4E: parentheses and brackets; 5.4F: up to two levels of grouping) and Common Core (5.OA.A.1: parentheses, brackets, or braces) call ( ) parentheses and [ ] brackets. Every lesson, key idea, worked example, quick check, explanation, deck, story and picture caption now says parentheses for ( ); where a factored form was meant, it now says factors or binomials, which is the exact math word.

The PEMDAS line had listed brackets and powers while naming PEMDAS; it now spells out Parentheses, Exponents, Multiply and Divide, Add and Subtract, and says exponents arrive in grade 6, as TEKS 5.4F keeps them out of grade 5.

  - order deck: steps: ['brackets', 'exponents', 'multiply and divide', 'add and subtract'] becomes steps: ['parentheses', 'exponents', 'multiply and divide', 'add and subtract']

Susanne Poulette Truesdale, who named whole body listening in 1990, calls it a tool, not a rule, and wrote in an update that its eye-contact part should be changed or dropped for autistic children. Social Thinking, which publishes the Whole Body Listening Larry books, is replacing the name with Listening with Brain and Body because the old one had become a standard of compliance; its note says some people listen better when they rock or move, look away from the speaker's face, or fidget. So the lesson told some children that the way they listen best is wrong. Retitled Listening with my brain and body, it now says your ears hear every sound and listening is your brain picking out the words to think about; that the body helps (turn toward the person, a quiet mouth until your turn, hands and feet to yourself so friends can listen too); and that children listen in different ways, some looking at the face, some looking down, some holding something soft. Painting P26 (children on a rug listening to their teacher in different ways) is logged for that line. The question about where your eyes look is gone; questions about the brain, turning toward the person and a girl who listens looking down take its place, and the bank grows from six questions to nine. Its source line quoted SL.K.2 without "or through other media" and now quotes it in full.

The lesson now gives the reason the end of a word matters: cat, cap and can start the same way, and only the last sound tells a friend which word you mean (in the story Theo says dig, so nobody hears dip). The second part of a telling is what it is like, which fits anything a child describes (it said what it does); speaking in whole sentences is said (TEKS (C), the conventions of language); loud enough is not a shout. Six questions become ten.

The values come as context, with the honest surprise that the smallest coin is not worth the least, and the faces are named truly (George Washington on the quarter, Abraham Lincoln on the penny, presidents long ago); every fact was checked against the U.S. Mint's specifications. Picture graphs (`picture-graphs-k`, K.8B and K.8C) teaches a real-object graph (the real things lined up in rows from one edge), a picture graph (one picture for each thing, so the graph stays after the toys are put away), and the conclusions a kindergartner draws: more, fewer, how many in each row, how many in all, how many more, and the most and fewest of three rows.

Graph questions say Look at this graph, so a pre-reader's question points at its picture, and explanations give the counting reason in the lesson's words (the row that reaches farther has more; count the pictures, the last number you say tells how many; match them one to one, the ones with no partner are the how many more). tools/untaught.mjs lists nothing for either module.

- People who shaped Texas and America (`people-who-shaped-us`, K.2): one true, plain contribution for each figure the standard names. George Washington led the army that won the country's freedom, was chosen as the first president, and is on the quarter and the dollar bill; Christopher Columbus sailed west from Spain in 1492 with three ships and reached islands in the Americas, where people already lived, and after him people from Europe came too, which changed life for everyone here in good ways and in hard ways; Stephen F. Austin brought about three hundred families to Texas when it was part of Mexico, is called the Father of Texas, and the capital is named for him; José Antonio Navarro, born in San Antonio, signed the Texas Declaration of Independence, helped write the first state constitution, spoke up for Tejanos so they could vote and own land, and has Navarro County named for him. Navarro's facts were read on the Texas Historical Commission's Casa Navarro page, the Texas State Cemetery's biography and Britannica Kids; the standard's own words name the four. Four paintings, one per figure (P45 to P48), one more than the usual three, since the standard names four; Columbus gets a ship scene with no close face, because no true likeness of him survives.

The Texas pledge keeps its semicolon, since quoted text is not ours to tidy. Questions ask what each word means and which word comes next; painting P49.
- Over, under, near and far (`near-far-left-right`, K.3A and K.3B): each spatial term on a picture (a table with a bird over it and a cat under it; a hill with a ball near a tree and a house far up the slope), left and right from the child's own hands, the school's places told from the front door on a drawn school map, and how to tell someone where a thing is. Painting P62.

Paintings P63 to P65.

## 2026-10-05 (pass KT): grade 1 Numbers to 20 at the full standard, and the grade 1 math earmark

- Mikey committed through KS and opened a new chat ("Committed through KS"), so the commit message starts fresh with KT. This pass is the first of the grade 1 review (Fable 5.1, not Opus 5.5, did it), in the review ledger's order: Numbers to 20, six modules, lesson, story and bank together, and the standards read in full before anything was cited.
- 19 TAC 111.3 (Grade 1, Adopted 2012) was read in full on TEA's site, and Common Core 1.OA and 1.NBT on thecorestandards.org. The plan had paraphrased four codes: 1.2B really says "compose and decompose numbers up to 120 in more than one way as so many hundreds, so many tens, and so many ones"; 1.2G names the symbols >, <, or =; 1.3B was cut off before "and unknowns as any one of the terms in the problem such as 2 + 4 = [ ]; 3 + [ ] = 7; and 5 = [ ] - 3"; 1.3D ends "decomposing a number leading to a 10". All four are quoted in full now, with 1.3A, 1.5C and 1.5F added for what Tens and ones and the two operations lessons teach, and 1.NBT.B.2 quoted with its three special cases. Writing numbers was mapped to 1.2B (composing and decomposing), which a tracing lesson does not teach; it moves to 1.2C (standard form) and 1.NBT.A.1 (read and write numerals).
- None of the six lessons had a spoken script, in a course that reads aloud to a child who is just learning to read, so a first grader heard the paragraphs read out. Each now has a script that teaches everything its questions ask, with prose paragraphs, a key idea and an example behind it. Teen numbers counts on from a full ten frame with the extra dots beside it (a new pair picture, ten and some more side by side, which the rules test now validates), reads the some more from the number's name, takes the ten away to find how many more than ten, says that eleven and twelve are built the same way, and says the next number is one more. Adding to 20 gives the reason for starting with the bigger number (fewer counts, and the turn-around fact that three and eight make eleven too), makes ten in two said steps, and finds a missing number in the middle or at the start of a sum. Subtracting to 20 counts back with the reason, takes away across ten in two steps (thirteen take away four is thirteen take away three, then one more, which the old lesson never taught though it cited 1.3D), says that subtracting undoes adding and turns ten take away eight into what do I add to eight, finds the missing number in the middle or at the start of a take-away, and compares two groups by matching in pairs. Tens and ones says a ten is a bundle of ten ones, that a number shows its tens first and its ones last, that thirty plus four equals thirty-four (1.3A, taught before and never cited), that the same number can be broken another way (two tens and fourteen ones, the "in more than one way" of 1.2B), that ten more and ten less change only the tens, and that ten tens make one hundred and the numbers go on past one hundred twenty. Bigger and smaller to 100 teaches greater than, less than and equal to beside bigger and smaller, and the three signs, each said by which way it opens; the old lesson showed 52 > 38 and never said what the sign meant. The sign lines start with Look, so the voice never reads a sign aloud. Writing numbers traces all ten digits, each told the way the app draws it, and then says how a two-digit number is written, tens digit first on the left (14 against 41).
- The question banks grew with seven kinds: the unknown at the start of a sum (? + 4 = 9, turned around and counted on), the unknown in the middle and at the start of a take-away (12 − ? = 5; ? − 4 = 8, found by adding), ten less, a ten plus a one-digit number (30 + 4), a number made another way (72 as 6 tens and 12 ones) and the sign between two numbers, with the three signs drawn large as choices. More, Less and The same became Greater than, Less than and Equal to, the comparative language the standard names. Every explanation now says the answer and the reason in whole sentences (count on from ten, one count for each extra dot; the first digit is the tens; the sign opens toward the bigger number), setups read as sentences, and the arithmetic of every new kind is re-derived by the rules test from the numbers in the words. Pools: Teen numbers 45 different questions, Adding to 20 735, Subtracting to 20 1,028, Tens and ones 644, Bigger and smaller 1,988, for rounds of five.
- Stories: Ten and three now counts on from a box of ten juice pouches, a thing that truly comes in ten, where it had counted on from an egg carton of ten, and most kitchens hold a carton of twelve; its five picture prompts and coloring page D114 follow. The Five said the five is drawn down first, around the belly, lift and across the top; the app draws it across the top, then down, then the belly, in one stroke, and the story and its picture S1638 now say so. The other four stories matched their lessons and stayed. Audio for the two changed stories was rebuilt from the words with their tags. No new paintings were logged: every line in this course carries an exact count, and a painted count that disagreed with the words would teach the wrong thing, so the app's own frames and dots stay the pictures.

The course teaches ten of the thirty-eight content expectations of 111.3 in full; no lesson teaches subitizing (1.2A), generating and ordering numbers with open number lines (1.2D, part of 1.2F), composing 10 with two or more addends (1.3C), explaining and generating problems (1.3E, 1.3F), coin values, the cent symbol and counting collections (1.4A to 1.4C), reciting and skip counting (1.5A, 1.5B), representing word problems with number sentences (1.5D), the equal sign and four-term equations (1.5E, part of 1.5F), properties of operations with three numbers (1.5G), all of geometry including halves and fourths (1.6A to 1.6H), length units and time to the hour and half hour (1.7A to 1.7E), and tally marks and picture and bar-type graphs (1.8A to 1.8C).
