## 2026-10-05 (pass KV): grade 1 Sky, water and living things at the full standard, and the grade 1 science earmark

- Mikey, after KU: "Continue, not committed", so KT, KU and KV share the commit message. This is the third grade 1 course in the review ledger's order, three modules, lesson, story and bank together (Fable 5.1).
- 19 TAC 112.3 (Science, Grade 1, Adopted 2021, effective April 26, 2022) was read in full on Cornell LII, and the NGSS performance expectations 1-ESS1-1, 1-ESS1-2, 1-LS1-1, K-LS1-1 and 2-PS1-4 were read in their published words. The plan was labeled 2021 and cited three codes that are not in that section: "1.8C, identify characteristics of the Sun and the Moon and describe their patterns" exists in no published text; "1.5B" and "1.9A" are the 2010 numbering, which the 2021 standard replaced. The same disease the grade 2 Magnets citation has (accuracy item A3) was in grade 1 too. The 2021 grade 1 standard has no Sun and Moon expectation at all; Texas teaches them in grade 2 (2.9A), and the grade 1 Earth and space expectation is the seasons (1.9), which no lesson teaches. So Patterns in the sky is cited to 1.5A (identify and use patterns to describe phenomena) and to NGSS 1-ESS1-1 and 1-ESS1-2, Water changes to 1.6B, 1.8A and 1.8B, and What animals need to 1.12A and 1.13A, every row quoted from the published text.
- The three lessons were four spoken lines each with no prose, and their banks could make six, five and five different questions for a round of five, the bare minimum. Each now has prose, a key idea, an example and a nine-line script. Patterns in the sky: the sun comes up in the east and goes down in the west every day, low in the morning and high at midday, and it only looks as if the sun moves because the Earth turns; a pattern is something that happens the same way again and again, so you can say what will happen tomorrow; the moon shines with sunlight and seems to change from a thin curve to half to full and back in about a month, and is sometimes up by day; stars come out at night in the same patterns and the bright sun hides them by day; long summer days and short winter days; never look straight at the sun. Water changes: ice is frozen water, heat melts it and cold freezes it again; boiling makes steam and steam cools back into drops; a puddle dries into the air; if you know what heat and cold do you can predict (an ice pop in the sun, a cup of water in the freezer); melted butter and candle wax harden again, and a cooked egg or a baked cake never goes back; a stove cooks, a dryer blows hot air, and hot things burn. What animals need: food, water, air and a safe place to live; living things grow and make young, and a toy does not; a fish uses its fins and gills and has scales, a bird its wings, feathers and beak, a dog its legs, fur, teeth and nose; where each lives; and people copy animal parts, a helmet from a shell, a coat from fur, swim fins from fins.
- The banks grew to twenty, eighteen and twenty-two different questions (sixteen new kinds), every explanation with its reason, and a star joined the question icons for the night-sky question. Every young-learner question names the picture it shows, and the two-answer sort of question stays at the pace of the course.

The expectations the lessons teach are (5)(B) (steady beat in excerpts from various periods and cultures), (6)(C) (same/different between beat/rhythm, higher/lower, louder/softer, faster/slower) and (1)(C) (the words allegro and largo for tempo and forte and piano for dynamics), which no lesson had taught, and the NCAS text MU:Re7.2.1a, which the plan had cut ("(such as beat or pitch)" and "for a purpose"), is quoted in full with MU:Re8.1.1a beside it.

Each lesson now has an eight-line script, prose, a key idea and an example drawn by the app. The steady beat teaches the beat as the even pulse under a song, kept with hands and feet; the rhythm as the pattern of long and short sounds on top, so beat and rhythm are told apart; tempo as the speed of the beat, with allegro for fast and largo for slow; and a beat in music from every time and place. High and low teaches pitch, bigger things usually lower, a child's voice higher than a grown-up's, the piano climbing to the right, a tune going up and down, and the voice sliding from a growl to a squeak. Loud and soft teaches dynamics with their jobs (a lullaby for one sleepy listener, a parade drum for a street), forte and piano and why the piano is called that (pianoforte, the first keyboard that could play both), and growing louder and fading as changes in dynamics and not in pitch or tempo. The banks grew to fourteen, eleven and eleven different questions with four new kinds, every choice a capitalized whole, and every explanation with its reason. The three stories already matched their lessons and stayed. No new paintings.

Flat shapes (1.6A, 1.6B, 1.6D) teaches sides and vertices as the words that name a shape, the rhombus and the hexagon beside the four kindergarten shapes, a square as a special rectangle and a special rhombus (both are true, and the lesson says why: four equal sides, and four square corners), what defines a shape and what does not (color, size, which way it turns), a tall thin triangle, a turned square and a stretched hexagon that keep their names, and sorting by the number of sides. Drawing shapes (1.6C) is a tracing module that draws all six, with rectangle, rhombus and hexagon strokes added to the pad, each said the way the strokes draw it. Solids and their faces (1.6E, 1.6B) teaches faces, edges and vertices, the rectangular prism with the cube as its special case the way a square is a special rectangle, the triangular prism with two triangle faces and three rectangle faces, the sphere, cylinder and cone with their flat faces counted, and the real things each is shaped like; a cone's point is never asked as a vertex, since books disagree on whether to count it. Joining shapes (1.6F) draws twelve composites, the same two triangles making a square, a bigger triangle, a rectangle or a rhombus depending on the join, squares making rectangles and a bigger square, three triangles a trapezoid (taught here, where the standard first needs it), six triangles or two trapezoids a hexagon, so the same target shape is made more than one way. Halves and fourths (1.6G, 1.6H, 1.G.A.3) teaches the whole, fair shares, halves and fourths with quarters as the other name, half of and fourth of, two halves and four fourths as the whole, the fourth smaller than the half of the same whole, halves cut three ways, and the non-examples, two or four pieces that are not the same size.

SolidPic draws the rectangular prism as a box longer than it is tall and the triangular prism as a tent. Two new picture kinds, shares (a circle, square or rectangle cut by name, with a shaded count) and joined (a composite drawn as its tinted pieces with the seams showing), and shares chips as tapped choices. Every drawing was rendered in the real built page and looked at; the cut shapes first drew with the dark theme's own colors and showed as black pieces, so they and the joined figures now use the paper palette like the other diagrams.

The rules test re-derives every kind from tables it does not share, and holds the inclusive rules: rectangle and rhombus are never offered as wrong names for a square, a square is never shown as a wrong picture when a rectangle or a rhombus is asked for, rectangular prism is never a wrong name for a cube, a cube is never a wrong picture for a rectangular prism, a piece set that can make the asked shape is never a wrong answer, and a yes-or-no about joining is checked against the table of what the pieces can make. Open number lines (1.2F, 1.2D, 1.NBT.B.3) teaches greater to the right and less to the left, an open line that shows only the numbers you need, counting the marks from a known number, a number between two numbers, which of two is farther right, ordering three numbers by tens then ones on the line, and counting on across a ten.

- The fourth exposure, as proposed to Mikey (not built; his call): a light review a few weeks after a lesson is mastered and its memory check passed, drawn from the same bank at the same difficulty, five questions, spoken for the early years. Timing by the forgetting curve: two to three weeks after the memory check, then, if passed, a second light review about six weeks later, and nothing more unless a later course needs the skill (where a memory check already reaches back across courses). Outcomes, three ways: a clear pass (four or five of five) ends the schedule for that lesson and the confidence score rises; a bare pass (three of five) keeps the schedule and brings the next review forward to one week with the misses re-asked first; a fail (two or fewer) sends the lesson back to practice at the full round, with its story offered again, and the lesson's prerequisites get one memory check each, since a fade that deep usually has a cause one step earlier. Nothing is shown to the child as a failure; the educator's report shows the lesson as "reviewing" with the date. Cost: no new content, one new round kind, one scheduler, educator settings to turn it off per student. If Mikey says yes, it becomes a pass of its own with its rules in ALGORITHMS.md and tests before any screen.

## 2026-10-07 (pass LU): First Steps (pre-K 4) part one at the refined standard: colors, same and different, the six matching lessons, more and fewer

- Mikey committed through LT. First Steps has eighteen modules, too many to review well in one pass, so it is split the way pass JR split it: part one here (Colors, Same and Different, the six matching lessons, More and Fewer), part two next (the sizes, Patterns, One, Two, Three, the three drawing lessons, Taking Turns and Helpers All Around), then the stories' tags and the course's long story.
- Angles. Each lesson gained two or three spoken lines that show its idea another way, each with a sentence in its prose. Colors: a stop sign, a blueberry, a lemon and a pickle beside the four anchors, sorting blocks by color, and naming the colors on your own clothes. Same and Different: a pair of socks, two red crayons from one box, and checking shape, color and size at cleanup time. Match the Vehicles: where each one goes (a car on the road, a train on a track, a boat on the water, a rocket into space), said aloud for the first time, and two cars outside. Match the Things: the butterfly's wings and the robot's arms and legs said aloud, and your own arms and legs. Match the Water Animals: how much bigger a whale really is than most fish, since the pictures draw them the same size, and the turtle, frog and duck named aloud. Match the Land Animals: the fox's pointy ears beside the cat's, the snail's one flat foot and the owl's big eyes, so every animal the matching questions show is now named in the lesson. Match the Shapes: shapes at home (most doors are rectangles, a window can be a square, a clock a circle) and a triangle drawn in the air. Match the Solids: all four solids beside their real things on the line the painting P17 already shows, a cylinder that rolls on its side and stands on its end, and rolling and stacking tried at home. More and Fewer: five fingers against two, snack plates, and lining two groups up one with one, where the group with some left over has more.

- Mikey committed through LU. This is the second half of First Steps' lessons and banks (pass LU did the first); the course's eighteen stories and its long story are next.
- Read against their standard. Both size lessons cite Texas Prekindergarten Guidelines V.D.1, which asks a child to compare heights or lengths of people or objects, and both taught only which thing takes up more room. Bigger and Smaller now teaches taller (towers that stand on the same floor) and longer (lines that start at the same place), and standing back to back with a friend to see who is taller (P114), and its questions now include the taller tower and the longer line, the kindergarten kinds, whose words the lesson now says. A cat between a mouse and a horse has its painting (P113). Big, Bigger, Biggest now says its own title's words, big, bigger, biggest, each one bigger than the one before (P115).
- Real sizes. A picture can show a bee and a bear the same size, so both size lessons now say so and name three groups: tiny (a bee, a snail), middle-sized (a cat, a rabbit, a duck, an owl, a fox) and huge (a bear, a whale) (P116). New kinds ask which of two animals is bigger or smaller in real life, and which of three is the biggest, the smallest or middle-sized. Only animals from different groups are compared, and a bear never meets a whale, since the smallest whales are about the size of a big bear. The setup line names the animals in alphabetical order and the pictures are shuffled on their own, so the bank counts each set of animals once; a first draft let the order vary, which counted every order as a new question and put Big, Bigger, Biggest at 369 when a child would meet 69.
- One, Two, Three. Its "How many?" kind had counted only to two in a lesson about three; a new kind asks one, two or three, dots or shapes. The lesson now counts on fingers and in claps, and says that things in a row or in a pile are each counted once. No painting, since a painted count could contradict the lesson.
- Patterns: a pattern with the body (clap, stomp, clap, stomp), beads on a string (P117), and one the child makes for a grown-up to guess. The three drawing lessons: lines in the world (rain falling in lines down, a table top across, lightning in a zigzag, P118, which takes that line off the picture-candidate list, now 32), each number said aloud on the way through the dots and the stars people joined with imagined lines to make pictures in the sky (P119), and the five shapes in real things (a button, a cracker, a slice of pizza, a card). Their banks are motor practice and stay as they are.
- Taking Turns names waiting as a feeling that can be hard and gives three things to do while you wait (a slow breath, counting to ten, cheering for a friend), with a swing to take turns on (P120). New kinds tell taking turns from sharing in a scene (one goes and then the other, or both at the same time) and choose what to do while waiting.
- Helpers All Around had no picture for the doctor, the teacher, the mail carrier or the police officer, and one line showed the firefighter, doctor and teacher chart while naming the mail carrier and the police officer. Each helper now has a line and a painting (P121 to P124), each says a little more (the fire truck, sick or hurt, reading stories, packages, cars on the street), two lines say where each helper works, and a last line says the child can be a helper too. New kinds ask who works where and which helper comes in a scene. The kindergarten courses share the old helper and good-choice kinds, so the new questions are kinds of their own and kindergarten's banks are unchanged.
- Banks: Bigger and Smaller 12 to 76 different questions, Big, Bigger, Biggest 9 to 69, One, Two, Three 20 to 36, Taking Turns 12 to 28, Helpers All Around 9 to 23; Patterns stays at 96. Eight new kinds, each re-derived in the rules test from its own words with tables the generators do not share; three were broken on purpose in a copy (the biggest and smallest swapped, a sharing scene called taking turns, the wrong helper at the post office), and the test failed on each. The new lesson lines and one practice round in each changed module were looked at in the real page at phone size: the towers stand together and the lines start together, each real-size question names its animals in a setup line the voice reads first, and the new paintings show their placeholders until Mikey makes them.

EARMARKS E12 places all 26 Approaches to Learning, Language and Communication, and Literacy goals (the Approaches to Learning goals, and the child's own talk, are a grown-up's or the classroom's), keeps only II.D.1's expressive half, people and events, and lists what Listen and Point now teaches and deliberately does not cite (P-MATH 4's first and second, P-MATH 10's spatial words, P-LC 7's sorting by color).
- Every finding below was read against its source before it was applied; where one was not applied, the reason is given.
- Round one, in parallel: the lesson brief (Listen and Point), the accuracy check (both courses' lessons and stories, and all 116 early-years experiments), the Wonder and game brief, the story brief (Very First Steps' twelve module stories), the story flow brief (eleven of them), the picture brief (both courses), and the screen and code briefs (Mikey's notes).
  - Lesson. Besides the citations above: Listen and Tap said "A pizza is round" over a drawn slice, "A bird has wings, so it can fly" (penguins and kiwis cannot), and named the moon and a cloud over a picture of the sun and a fish side by side, so nothing was up or down; it never said "listen to the word, then find its picture", its key idea's second half. Which One Is Different? showed two things where "different" means unlike the others, never sorted though it cited sorting, and drew the shape to match larger than its twin, which by its own size line made both choices different. Circle and Square defined a square by its corners alone and told a child that many windows are square. Every bank was mostly recall: Circle and Square's 16 were 4 tasks recolored, every round repeating one; Which One Is Different?'s 72 were one task re-dressed, always unlike in shape and color together; Listen and Tap had 10 and Animal Sounds 12, all naming what was just heard; A and B's explanations said the question back; and five of the course's eight generators had no re-derivation in the rules test. The fixes: a square is "four corners, and its four sides are all the same length", a little square and a square turned on its corner are still squares, and size does not change the shape (V.C.4); a ball rolls and a block does not; "Many plates are round like a circle, and some windows are square." Which One Is Different? shows rows of three, says different can be the color, the shape or the size, and sorts by color (V.E.1), with a reason on the apple line. Listen and Tap says "This is a slice of pizza. We cut a pizza into slices to eat it.", "A bird has wings, and most birds can fly.", shows the sun, the moon and the clouds up in the sky and then the sun stacked over a fish down in the water (P100 moves to that line), and ends "When you practice, listen to the word, then find its picture and tap it." Animal Sounds adds that hearing tells you what is near and which sound came first and which second. Eleven new question kinds, each with its re-derivation: the shape by its corners, the real thing round like a circle or with corners like a square, the same shape at another size or turn; the odd one out by color, by shape and by size alone; the one that does not go with a group sorted by color; a picture found by what the lesson says it does or where it is; up in the sky or down in the water; which animal came first or second; and one of two sounds heard at once. A and B explains by the letter's look. Bank sizes are at the end.
  - Accuracy, Listen and Point and Very First Steps: the bird, the pizza and the windows (above, the same fixes), and Two Shoes sent Lena and her dad out in one shoe each (now two pairs). Its suggestions taken: real animals make lots of sounds, a block "does not roll" (on a slope it slides) rather than sits still, "Many words name things" (not every word names a thing), the tree known by its trunk, and CS619 drawing Mike at three. Its notes on the stories (a three-year-old alone in tall grass, where ticks wait; a hot pizza; a quote not credited; a boy who went home alone) went into the story rewrites below.
  - Accuracy, the experiments: all 116 ideas for pre-K 3 to grade 2 read as a careful parent would, with AAP, CPSC, Poison Control, Shriners, CDC and FDA sources. Twenty-seven had to change (eight for pre-K 3, five for pre-K 4, three for kindergarten, six for grade 1, five for grade 2; pre-K 4's two copies of Rain in a Jar counted once): coins, a wine cork, buttons, a pebble, dried beans in a tub a child can open, and a small toy, for three-year-olds (the AAP's choking list and the CPSC small-parts cylinder); a bucket of water; vinegar in a dropper; latex balloons, a choking risk to age eight (AAP, CPSC); hot water, hot syrup and steam over a boiling pot (scalds, Shriners); peanut butter (an FDA major allergen, in schools); a paper pinwheel on a pin (the CPSC sharp-point rule, under eight); a child slicing vegetables; a bag of mold opened near a child (CDC); a parking lot (NHTSA); a bug looked at closely where fire ants live (Texas A&M AgriLife); "mark where the sun comes up" (looking at the sun); a seed's root that the idea said comes after its sprout (it comes first, UF/IFAS); an order of melting that depends on sizes and places; and an hour's watch in which a plant cannot be seen to grow, so it acts like the rock beside it (now a few days, and hands washed after the snail, CDC). About forty more small changes were taken. A safety line now heads the experiments (below).
  - Wonder and game. w-same-or-different's scientist ended "so the honest answer is both" on a screen that says no answer is right, and his short voice said the same; Chloe called a one-color picture a wall; Georgette had no faith of her own; Mike tested nothing; and the prompt, "Are you the same as your friend", assumed a friend. All rewritten (quoted below). In w-big-or-small, Mike's proposed rewrite ("so I would not take either one on trust") had a three-year-old doubt a grown-up's "too small", which is how a safety limit is said; it ships reworded. The game: Listen and Point owned Red and Blue, a sort by color it never taught, while Very First Steps' Red and Blue lesson teaches it word for word, so Red and Blue moves to Very First Steps, and Listen and Point gets a new game, Step on the Circles (path-circles, a circle-square deck: circles and squares in the same four colors, so only the shape moves the dot to the star). Found along the way: Catch the Hexagons (grade 1) had never drawn a hexagon, since every chip shape but a circle, a square and a diamond fell back to a triangle; SvgChip now draws the hexagon and the rhombus.
  - Story, Very First Steps. Ten of its twelve stories were rewritten so each teaches what its lesson does and what the printed book lists under it, with a real turn, a grown-up to say each rule, and no general fact in the narrator's voice; The Other Mitten (read whole after MA) and Two Plates stand. Two Balls became Two Buckets: Mia and Sam sort red balls and blue balls into two buckets with Mia's mom there, and nobody goes home alone. Like Me? became There You Are!: Little Fox, looking for her brother, takes an owl for him until she sees its big round eyes and no pointy ears, and when her brother comes, the same in ears, eyes and color, the owl names himself the odd one out (the old story matched a duckling by its peep, and had a hen and a goat the lesson never names). One Small Bed compares height side by side and length from the same end, with no "light". Splash: Grandpa draws 1 and 2 in the dirt, says to point to each duck and that the last number tells how many, and Nell counts moving ducks. The First Line: Kai starts in the middle and runs off the page, then Mom makes a dot at the top and says where to start (the old story celebrated starting anywhere and ended on an uncredited Paul Klee line). One, Two, Three became Dot to Dot: four dots joined out of order cross, and in order, by the numerals 1 to 4 Dad writes, they make a boat. Where Is the Frog?: Grandma finds Theo's yellow toy duck in the green grass at once and says why (the colors are different), so Theo hides his green frog there, and she cannot find it; then he sorts his bath toys by color. Pizza Corners: Diego skips a little triangle, Dad says big or little it is still a triangle, and the moral has three straight sides. Two Shoes: two pairs. May I, Please?: Gus and Mira, new names, with Miss Hazel there. No lead child's name repeats in the course.
  - Story flow, on the old stories: three even runs across page breaks and a few grown-up phrases; the rewrites replaced those versions, and the new text went to the flow check in round two.
  - Picture. Forty-one of Very First Steps' forty-eight story rows were the batch tool's (prompt = alt + style), so Leonardo, which never sees the paragraph, would get names, "the girl" with no age, "the yellow duck" with no toy, "dot one" against a ban on numbers, and counts with no check note. The ten rebuilt stories' forty rows were written by hand to the brief, and twenty more rows were rewritten as it proposed (among them P98's plate seen straight on as a full circle beside a truly square window, P99's one red apple among green ones all one size and plain green, and P92 and P127 with size check notes, P127 exactly two shoes), with ", sun" in the negative prompt of the color lessons' outdoor pictures.
  - Screen and code, on Mikey's notes: the tour's card 8 (above); What's new and the reminder out of sight in a page-tall frame; a replayed tour opening over waiting news; a read during a loop back counted as elective; Copy throwing the keyboard focus onto the page; and a build older than its source. - Round two, second reads by the same seven.
  - Lesson: the sorting line "When we sort, the things that are the same go together" stood over a red circle grouped with a red square, which the lesson's own "same" (look just alike) calls different, so it says "Let's sort by color. Things that are the same color go together.", and the key idea and The Apple Puzzle follow; "Tap the one we cut into slices to eat" could offer the fish or the bird, and "down in the water" the bird (a duck swims), now never; the tree line named branches the drawn tree does not show (and a palm has none), so "A tree grows tall, with a trunk."; and "When you hear two sounds, one comes first and one comes second" was false of two at once, so "When one sound comes after another, one is first and the other is second." From its suggestions: P16 is a red ball rolling alone (the block was named a line later); the growling bear never makes "two animals are near"; the odd color is never red against green, the most common color vision deficiency (MedlinePlus); Very First Steps' Triangles defines a square by its equal sides too (pass KH), and grade 1's Read the Word says "Many words name a thing, a color, a number or a shape" (pass KF); E12 quotes P-LC 7 whole and places P-MATH 10's second sentence (read again on headstart.gov). Recorded clips of these lessons, if any were made outside the repository, must be made again, since every line after an inserted one moved its clip key.
  - Accuracy: the new safety line said hot or deep water needs a grown-up, while a young child can drown in an inch or two (AAP), so it now reads "Read each idea through before you start, and keep a grown-up nearby. Young children do every idea with a grown-up beside them. Small things and balloons can choke a young child, and even an inch or two of water can drown one, so stay within arm's reach of any water and keep hot water in grown-up hands." (worded for every grade, the screen check's point); Splash's duck that "came down from the sky" was painted as a white farm duck, and most farm ducks cannot fly (National Geographic), so the newcomer is a wild mallard. Its correction to round one: the AAP lists raw apple pieces among foods to keep from children under four, and no pre-K 3 child eats a raw apple now (The Apple Puzzle sorts its apples instead). From its suggestions: "an owl may be near" (a daytime hoot is most likely a mourning dove, Audubon), the Sun and Moon Chart says "Each time you can see the moon, at night or in the day, draw it." (NASA: some nights it is up only by day), the bird feeder's seed has no nuts, Georgette ties three-year-old Mike's shoe, the shadow moved "because the sun seemed to move across the sky", a picnic sandwich is "almost a triangle", and Tooth in Soda uses a hard-boiled egg, shell on.

- Wonder edits, shipped under Mikey's MB rule and quoted for his later check. Since an educator's approval is kept by the question's id, they reach classrooms that already approved these questions (the open question in RULES-AUDIT section 11 now has a live case).
  - w-same-or-different, the prompt, was: "Are you the same as your friend, or different?" Now: "Are you and a friend the same, or different?"
  - Frederick (The Scientist), short, was: "Everyone is a little the same and a little different." Now: "Let's test it! Ask a friend their favorite food, and listen. Is it your favorite too?"
  - Chloe (The Artist), short, was: "Different is what makes a picture interesting." Now: "When I paint two friends, I look for what matches, and then for what does not."
  - Frederick, was: "Every person shares almost everything with every other person, and still no two are alike. Both things are true at once, so the honest answer is both." Now: "Before I answer a question like this, I collect evidence. Ask a friend about their favorite food, game and song, and listen closely to each answer. Make two lists, one for what matches and one for what does not, and see what your lists tell you."
  - Chloe, was: "A picture made of one color is a wall. Art needs sameness to hold together and difference to be worth looking at. Friendships are a lot like that." Now: "When I paint two friends, I look twice. The first time I notice what matches, the same muddy boots or the same big smile. The second time I notice what does not, and that is how each face ends up looking like nobody else."
  - Georgette (The Grandparent of Faith), was: "Old stories are full of friends who were nothing alike and loved each other anyway. The differences were usually the point of the story." Now: "My faith teaches me that every person is made with care, and that no two are made the same. So when I meet someone very different from me, I look for what I can learn from them, and I always find something."
  - Mike (The Skeptic), was: "You will notice ways you and a friend are different, and noticing is fine. Different does not mean better or worse. It just means not the same." Now: "The same in what way? You and a friend might laugh at the same jokes and go to bed at different times, so I check one thing at a time. I keep my answer in pencil, because friends grow and change. If anyone says different means better or worse, I ask them how they know."
  - w-big-or-small, Georgette, was (the approved text): "Old stories are full of small ones who did big things. Being small has never meant being unimportant, and every grandparent knows it." Now, as pass MA proposed: "The old stories I love, some of them from my faith, are full of small ones who did big things. I have always believed that being small never means being unimportant."
  - w-big-or-small, Mike, was (the approved text): "Grown-ups sometimes say you are big and sometimes say you are small. Both can be true at once. It is one of the first questions with more than one good answer." Now, not the wording pass MA proposed: "Grown-ups call you big one day and too small the next, and I used to wonder which one was true. Now I ask, big enough for what? Big enough to carry your plate is not the same as big enough to drive. It is one of the first questions with more than one good answer."
  - Standing under the rule, already live: w-big-or-small's theme (world) and Frederick's line there (pass MA), and w-early-lost-my-turn's brain-and-body line (pass LY).
